Deep Dive
High-Level Overview
Orchard Robotics is a California-based agtech startup founded in 2022 that builds AI-powered camera systems and software to provide precise data on fruit crops, enabling farmers to optimize management decisions. Its core product, FruitScope, mounts on tractors or farm vehicles to capture high-resolution images analyzed by AI for metrics like fruit size, color, count, and health, feeding into Vault, a cloud-based system-of-record for farm operations. The company serves large-scale growers of apples, grapes, blueberries, cherries, almonds, pistachios, citrus, and strawberries, solving the critical lack of actionable data that forces multi-million-dollar decisions based on manual sampling and guesswork. With $22 million in oversubscribed Series A funding announced in September 2025 (bringing total capital to over $25 million), Orchard is doubling its team and opening a San Francisco office to fuel expansion, already deployed on major U.S. farms.
Origin Story
Orchard Robotics was founded in 2022 by Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow and Cornell University computer science dropout, inspired by his grandparents' apple farming in China. While at Cornell—a leading agriculture school—Wu connected with top fruit experts, uncovering how even the largest U.S. farms relied on imprecise manual inspections for critical decisions on labor, inputs, and management. He spun the company out of Cornell, initially raising $3.8 million in pre-seed and seed rounds led by Contrary and backed by General Catalyst, achieving early traction with leading apple and grape farms. This marked a pivotal shift from legacy farming challenges to scalable AI-driven precision, addressing long sales cycles and slow innovation in agtech.
Core Differentiators
Role in the Broader Tech Landscape
Orchard rides the precision agriculture wave, leveraging advances in machine learning, computer vision, and edge computing to make per-fruit data accessible beyond mega-farms—a breakthrough enabled only in the last five years. Timing aligns with escalating pressures on U.S. specialty crop growers: labor shortages, rising input costs, climate variability, and supply chain demands for yield predictability, where imprecise data bottlenecks multi-million decisions. Market forces like farm consolidation and tech adoption favor Orchard, positioning it to influence agtech by automating workflows and enabling sustainable practices—potentially expanding the $100B+ specialty crops market through data-driven efficiency. As an "AI farming company," it humanizes tech for an industry long left behind by innovation hurdles, fostering ecosystem-wide shifts toward profitable, resilient operations.
Quick Take & Future Outlook
Orchard Robotics is poised to dominate precision ag for orchards and vines, using its $25M+ war chest to scale FruitScope/Vault globally and build the full "farm OS" for end-to-end automation. Key trends like AI maturation, autonomous equipment integration, and sustainability mandates will accelerate adoption, potentially capturing workflows from scouting to sales. Its influence could evolve from data provider to indispensable platform, owning farm decisions amid competitors' consolidations—echoing its founding vision to secure America's food supply through tech that finally makes farming efficient and profitable.

Orchard Robotics Brings AI to Farming, Optimizes Every Crop
FruitScope OS gives growers a complete view of their operations and integrates seamlessly with existing farm processes to deliver a unified management experience.
By   Donna Joseph   
Dec 24, 2025 11:56 PM
Orchard Robotics Brings AI to Farming, Optimizes Every Crop Photo by SBR
Summary
 Orchard Robotics, based in San Francisco, California, is developing AI-powered solutions to automate farms, helping growers increase profitability, efficiency, and sustainability while addressing the lack of precise, field-level data in modern agriculture.
 The FruitScope platform, including Vision, Vault, and OS, provides comprehensive farm data collection, management, and analysis. Farmers can track billions of fruit across millions of trees, vines, or plants and make informed decisions across all farm operations, from planting and irrigation to harvesting and distribution.
 Canary, Orchard’s AI engine, leverages one of the largest agricultural datasets in the world to optimize farm decision-making. By analyzing millions of trees simultaneously, it automates and improves efficiency and profitability, enabling fully data-driven, AI-powered farm management.
SAN FRANCISCO, Calif., Oct. 25, 2025 — FarmTech company Orchard Robotics is working to secure America’s food supply by building an AI farmer that automates farms. By working closely with growers, the company aims to make farming profitable, efficient, and sustainable again.
FruitScope Vision is Orchard’s industry-leading AI-powered camera system. It can be mounted on any tractor or farm vehicle and captures precise data for every crop on every tree, vine, or plant throughout the season. Built with best-in-class, farm-tough hardware and advanced artificial intelligence, the system delivers reliable results at scale, supporting operations from 100 acres to more than 10,000 acres.
FruitScope Vault serves as a system of record for a farm’s most valuable data. Designed from the ground up, it streamlines critical information and integrates it into decision-making across the farm. The platform helps track billions of fruit across tens of millions of trees, vines, or plants over multiple seasons.
FruitScope OS is Orchard’s modern farm management software suite, where data meets decision-making. The platform allows farmers to view and act on all their farm data through a single interface. According to the company, data is only valuable if it can be used, and automation is only possible when farmers fully understand what is happening in the field. Every decision, from pruning and spraying to irrigation, hiring, harvesting, marketing, selling, and distribution, depends on knowing what is growing in the field.
Canary is Orchard’s core AI engine that powers decision-making across the entire farm. Built on some of the largest agricultural datasets in the world, Canary learns from millions of trees and their outcomes to automate and optimize farm decisions, helping growers achieve higher profitability and efficiency while maintaining sustainability.
Founded in 2022 by Thiel Fellow Charlie Wu, Orchard Robotics is addressing one of modern agriculture’s biggest challenges, the lack of precise, field-level data.
How Orchard Supports Progressive Farmers
Fully Automated Farms: Orchard envisions a future where farms operate very differently from today. In this future, AI continuously gathers data on every plant and autonomously makes decisions that lead to better crop outcomes. The company notes that automation is not immediate and requires first identifying inefficiencies and then applying data in practical ways. Orchard is laying the groundwork of systems, data, and software to make this future possible.
Full Farm Data: FruitScope Vision provides thorough, precise, and accurate data collection throughout the growing season. Farmers can understand every tree, vine, or plant across large operations spanning multiple blocks, ranches, and seasons. Orchard emphasizes that modern software is essential to bridge the gap between field data and farm management, allowing growers to integrate insights directly into existing workflows.
AI-Powered Decision-Making: Orchard’s AI analyzes millions of trees simultaneously to uncover the most efficient and profitable management strategies. Data forms the foundation of every farming decision, and usable data is essential for automation. FruitScope OS gives growers a complete view of their operations and integrates seamlessly with existing farm processes to deliver a unified management experience.

Funding to Strengthen America’s Food Supply
In September, Orchard Robotics announced an oversubscribed 22-million-dollar Series A funding round. The round was led by Quiet Capital and Shine Capital, with continued participation from General Catalyst, Contrary, Mythos, Valyrian, Ravelin, and other investors, including Formula One World Champion Nico Rosberg and Yext and Roam founder Howard Lerman. The funding brings the company’s total capital raised to more than 25 million dollars.
Today, even the largest farms often rely on manual sampling that covers less than 0.01 percent of their crops to make high-value decisions related to labor, inputs, management, sales, and supply chains. This data gap results in inefficiencies and economic losses at a time when labor and input costs are rising and farm efficiency has stalled.
Charlie Wu notes that agriculture has not fundamentally evolved in the past two decades despite sharp cost increases. He describes farming as a data problem, where the lack of precise and actionable information limits progress. Orchard Robotics, he says, exists to help farmers operate more profitably and efficiently, and the new funding supports that mission.

Farm robotics in the weeds as funding declines 36% from Q2 to Q3

A robotic "Beehome" from Beewise. Image credit: Beewise
[Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company is AgFunder.]
Venture capital funding for agrifood robotics and mechanization is down again, dropping 36% from $168 million in Q2 to $108 million in Q3, according to preliminary data from AgFunder.
The latter figure also represents a 57% year-over-year decline vs Q3 2024, when the AgFunder-defined Robotics, Mechanization & Equipment category raised $252 million across 11 deals.
Funding for the category for all of 2025 so far is $412 million.
All of these numbers are in line with the rest of agrifoodtech funding for Q3, which was down 32% from the previous quarter. That drop is almost a 50% decrease from Q3 2024.

The Robotics, Mechanization & Equipment category includes on-farm machinery, automation tools, and drones.
While funding to the category is down, it’s important to reiterate the figures are preliminary, based on currently available data. These numbers could likely increase in the coming weeks as more data becomes available.

Top rounds: Q1–Q3 2025
Weed control remains the top area for ag robotics, and multiple companies addressing it raised funds this year.

One is Australia’s SwarmFarm Robotics, which raised $30 million. Its autonomous machines and corresponding software are, relative to most farming equipment, lightweight, versatile, and easily programmable. The company’s bread and butter continues to be weeding, but in recent years it has also branched out into precision application of crop protection products as well as slashing and mowing.
Numerous other startups are addressing the weed management issue through various technologies, from laser weeders to thermal micro-jetting. Those who raised funding in 2025 so far include TRIC Robotics, Rootwave, and Red Barn Robotics.
Outside of weeding, another compelling company is Beewise. Its solar-powered “Beehome” illustrates the role AI and automation can play in reversing bee colony losses, which remain higher than average in 2025.
Beewise says its Beehomes enable more precise, around-the-clock monitoring of bee hives and health, and can help hives stave off harm from monoculture health problems, chemical inputs, and other threats.
Funding by region: Q1–Q3 2025
North America, and the United States in particular, continues to lead funding for the category. For the first three quarters of 2025, it was followed by Asia (including Israel), then Europe.
In North America, the bulk of deals came from US-based startups, with just one (4AG Robotics’ Series B) round from Canada. US companies came from a variety of states across the country.
Nearly half of Asia’s $110 million in funding went to Beewise’s $50 million Series D round. There were also a number of undisclosed rounds from Asian startups in Q3.

‘Increasingly integral to modern agriculture’
This week also marked the launch of The Mixing Bowl’s 2025 Crop Robotics Landscape, the latest version of the organization’s ongoing market map series.
The Mixing Bowl noted a “continued evolution” across the crop robotics sector. New entrants, maturing technologies, and a growing convergence of robotics, sensing, and artificial intelligence reflect an ecosystem that is dynamic and increasingly integral to modern agriculture.
“Compared to 2024, the new Landscape shows continued traction in autonomy for row crops, stronger commercial activity in weeding, and an increased pipeline of startups offering autonomous tractors, smaller platform/carriers, and scouting and application drones.”

Nature Robots lands €4 million to automate organic and regenerative agriculture
Lucy Ngige · March 31, 2026
 LinkedIn
 X
 Email
Gift this article
Share this story with anyone — no subscription required.

Credit: Nature Robots
Regenerative agriculture practices, such as weed control that would otherwise be handled by spraying chemicals, can be labor intensive, as even a casual gardener can attest. With nearly 40% of farmers in Germany aged 55 or older, that’s a lot of aching backs.
Nature Robots, a spin-off from the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, makes software and autonomous field robots for precision agriculture for use on organic, regenerative agriculture and photovoltaic farms and vineyards.
The startup raised €4 million ($4.5 million) in seed funding from Climentum Capital, Bayern Kapital, and food-focused Planetary Impact Ventures. Its software maps plants to identify crop stress, enables 3D navigation, and eliminates weeds with precision lasers, which the company says reduces chemical inputs by up to 90%.
“Our autonomy platform enables machinery manufacturers to embark on the necessary transformation very quickly without having to invest billions in in-house development,” said Nature Robots’ Sebastian Pütz.
Blended
Nature Robots last year landed €6.5 million, including €4 million in equity, from the European Innovation Council Accelerator.The ag robotics sector has seen funding grow from $837 million in 2024 to $898 million last year. Switzerland-based Ecorobotix recorded 2025’s largest deal, raising $105 million in a series D round. US-based maker of humanoid robots Beyond Imagination, which has applications in agriculture and surgical assistance, raised $100 million.
Other notable raises include Greece-based Terra Robotics which landed €1.8 million for laser weeding, US-based automation company for vineyardsOrchard Robotics which raised $22 million last year, Norway-based Saga Robotics with €9.5 million and Denmark-based FarmDroid which landed €10.5 million for its solar-powered farm robots.

raw_content:
Jonathan Shriftman
Robotics Deep Dive: How Physical AI Is Winning Without a "ChatGPT Moment"
I interviewed founders building robots—humanoids, warehouses, farms, fabs. Everyone's waiting for robotics "ChatGPT moment." The operators deploying at scale say it's not coming. And that's better.
Jonathan Shriftman
Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
Introduction
Over the past two years, I’ve been writing about and investing some in the resurgence of American manufacturing. Within that, robotics emerged as a critical area to examine further, not just within manufacturing, but also across the broader economy.
To be candid, I’ve looked at dozens of robotics deals over the last year, but didn’t have conviction on where category winners would emerge or how the landscape was shaping up.
So I set out to change that and understand whether robotics could finally close the gap between decades of Jetson’s style hype and real-world impact.
The timing feels right…
In just the past month—January through early February 2026—robotics and physical AI has seen monumental fundraises: Skild AI raised $1.4B to build a general-purpose “robot brain,” Physical Intelligence pulled in $400M for generalist models, Bedrock Robotics secured $270M for autonomous heavy construction equipment, Mytra raised $120M for warehouse systems, and RobCo closed $100M to scale modular industrial robots for SMEs.
To make sense of this inflection, I interviewed founders across humanoids (Agility Robotics), warehouses and manufacturing (Locus Robotics, Ambi Robotics, Dexterity, Formic), and vertical specialists (Miso Robotics, Orchard Robotics, Bright Machines), and an investor at Goldman Sachs Growth Equity who covers the space.
Here’s what I learned. Three forces are converging;
The buyer is ready. Labor shortages, turnover, injuries, and rising wages have turned robotics from a pilot project into a practical staffing solution. Companies aren’t chasing innovation, they’re literally just trying to keep the line running.
The business model has changed. Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS) killed the two biggest barriers: upfront capital and technical risk. Now, robots are like software, it’s a monthly subscription with deployment, maintenance, and uptime guarantees baked in. Companies buy an outcome, not a machine.
The technology is ACTUALLY delivering. Robot companies are running fleets at scale, in real conditions, with boring reliability (this is a good thing). And like Tesla’s data advantage in FSD, deployed fleets compound: more robots means more data, better systems, faster deployment.
My main takeaway: robotics isn’t waiting for a “ChatGPT moment”, and it’s unclear to me if we’ll have one. One founder described it as more of a “snowball.”
My sentiment is the inflection is operational. What do I mean? The winners will be the ones that get robots into production fastest, run them with enterprise-grade uptime, and turn deployments into compounding data and distribution advantages.
There’s also an emerging question about which models will win—hyper-horizontal, hyper-vertical, or completely general. I’ll dig into that below as I present a few opinionated investment theses.
But first, a word on stakes.
Saman Farid, founder at Formic, a company that deploys robots as pay-per-part service, not capital purchase, put it simply: “Greatness is when humanity is liberated from drudgery, when abundance is instantly available to all.” That’s what’s at play here.
Let’s get into it.
Why Now?
Structural Labor Crisis Is Creating Real Demand
Manufacturing has roughly 415,000 unfilled jobs today, with nearly 1.9 million projected to remain open through 2033. But the problem extends beyond factories: 76% of logistics operations report labor shortages—many companies are replacing entire workforces more than once per year.
The pressure is compounding. A quarter of manufacturing workers are nearing retirement while wages continue to rise. Companies face availability constraints and cost pressure simultaneously. The founders I spoke with described this from the front lines.
Jeff Mahler, Co-founder & CTO of Ambi Robotics (robotic sorting for warehouse and logistics automation), pointed to the human cost: “Workers are exposed to repetitive and injury-prone motions,” which “creates high turnover, leading to a labor shortage in the industry.”
Richard Hull, CEO of Miso Robotics (kitchen robots for fast-food cooking and prep), was more blunt. The fry station is “their hardest-to-staff, most dangerous position” and “the number one workers’ comp claim in restaurants.” Nearly 80% of fast-food workers report burn injuries. Labor turnover exceeds 144% annually, says Richard.
Miso Robotics
Saman Farid, CEO of Formic (which employees the RaaS model for industrial robot arms for palletizing, machine tending, and assembly), described the same dynamic as a system-wide staffing breakdown: “Manufacturing faces a large and painful labor shortage.” One customer “hired more than 250 people in a single year just to keep ~100 roles filled.” The real cost is churn—”those 12 palletizing jobs are getting turned over four times a year… which is 60 people.”
Sviat Dulianov, CEO of Bright Machines (a software-defined robot that automates production of complex electronics, especially AI and data-center infrastructure) says: “the only scalable answer is to replace skill with software/AI and replace scale with robots that can run 24/7.”
The takeaway is simple: operators aren’t buying robotics to be innovative. They’re buying it because the line has to run, and the old staffing model is failing.
Robotics-as-a-Service Changes Adoption Economics
The business model has changed in a way that matters more than most people realize. The new model is RaaS; Robotics-as-a-Service.
Robotics is no longer sold as equipment you buy and hope you can operate. It’s increasingly delivered as a service like software with an ongoing relationship where the vendor is responsible for making the system work in production. This shift removes the two biggest barriers to adoption: upfront capital and technical risk.
The founders I spoke with described how this plays out in practice.
Charlie Wu, CEO of Orchard Robotics (autonomous robots for precision agriculture and orchard management), underscored why this reliability matters so much to customers operating on thin margins: “We can extract the hardware out of the equation just focus on the value prop. By adding our system, for our customers, if we can reduce cost by 1%, sometimes that can mean 2x in their profit.”
Orchard Robotics
Jonathan Hurst, Co-founder and CTO of Agility Robotics (bipedal humanoid robots for warehouse logistics and material handling), put it starkly: “RaaS is about risk reduction for the customers. Our contract doesn’t even mention robots. It just commits to moving X totes per hour with Y reliability.”
Agility Robotics
Dustin Pederson, CFO of Locus Robotics (autonomous mobile robots for warehouse order fulfillment and picking), described it as a “subscription business model” designed to “make it easy for customers to adopt automation,” with the flexibility to “scale up or down” as demand changes.
Locus Robotics
Saman Farid at Formic calls it “Full Service Automation,” where “we own the entire lifecycle—from engineering and deployment to uptime, service, and continuous improvement.” The reason is simple: “Most factories are not equipped to buy, own, manage, and service robots on their own.”
Formic
The upshot: Robots-as-a-Service is turning robotics into something closer to infrastructure. You’re not buying a machine—you’re buying an outcome with accountability baked in.
Reliable Technology
The technology is maturing in a way that’s visible on the ground: robots are moving from prototype to dependable production system.
What separates the leaders isn’t the flashiest demo—it’s boring reliability, earned through repetition at scale. And that reliability creates a compounding advantage.
Charlie Wu from Orchard Robotics described how this compounding plays out in practice: “It took us two years to get really good at apples. It took us three months to get really good at grapes. It took us three weeks to get really good at cherries.”
Saman Farid at Formic made the analogy explicit: “Our existing fleet of robots is collecting more data every minute, every hour, every day. It’s similar to Tesla having the benefit in FSD of having millions of cars on the road collecting data points.”
Jeff Mahler at Ambi Robotics put it plainly: “The best way to get this data is from real-world deployments. The more real-world deployments a company has, the more ‘on-policy’ data they have to achieve very high levels of reliability and performance. This advantage compounds because production data creates a flywheel where AI improves, opening new opportunities to automate adjacent tasks, and builds the company’s reputation for high performance in production, helping to close other customers.
Ambi Robotics
Dustin Pederson at Locus Robotics described the same flywheel: “More systems deployed lead to more data. More real-world, chaotic data leads to better training, better fleet performance—which leads to more value to the customer.”
Samir from Dexterity shared, “We obsess over trust and safety for Physical AI. Our Physical AI systems are trained for safety and interpretability. They meet the highest standards of performance, reliability and safety at the largest customers in the world. This is very difficult and takes many years to achieve, which is a significant and compounding advantage.”
The pattern is clear: deployed fleets aren’t just revenue—they’re a data moat that accelerates everything else.
Understanding Form Factor
The way that I’ve thought about this is understanding the robotics landscape starts with separating the stack into three layers: foundation models (the AI “brains” that enable perception, decision-making, and action), hardware platforms (the physical robots, differentiated by form factor), and application-layer companies (which deploy these systems into specific industries and workflows).
Layer 1: Foundation Models
Foundation model companies build AI systems designed to power any robot—analogous to how OpenAI and Anthropic build language models that power many applications. These models pre-train on massive datasets (human videos, physics simulations, robot manipulation data) then fine-tune for specific tasks.
The key advance is generalization. Rather than programming each task explicitly, models learn transferable manipulation primitives—how to grasp, move, apply force, and recover from failure. Adapting a robot to a new task can now require hours of data instead of weeks of manual programming.
Skild AI is training large-scale models on video, simulation, and robot interaction data to enable broad generalization across embodiments. Physical Intelligence builds embodiment-agnostic action models that learn reusable manipulation primitives, allowing robots to adapt to new tasks with minimal additional data. Field AI focuses on autonomy and foundation models for robots operating in unstructured, outdoor, and industrial environments where edge cases dominate. Cobot applies learning-based control and demonstration to make collaborative robots faster to deploy and easier to re-task in factories. Generalist AI is pursuing broadly capable robotic intelligence that can transfer skills across many tasks and domains, reducing the need for task-specific engineering.
While foundation models lower the cost and time to adapt, they don’t eliminate the challenges of real-world deployment…. Reliability, edge cases, and production-grade performance remain constrained by hardware, environment, and integration.
Jeff from Ambi gave this analogy: “Just like humans, robots need practice doing a particular task of interest in their own bodies before they work with high levels of reliability. If you’re learning to play golf, you can’t just watch videos and then go hit the course and expect to be Tiger Woods. You need to actually practice yourself, in your own body.”
Layer 2: Hardware Platforms
Robots come in different physical forms, each optimized for specific environments and economics. Form factor determines where a robot can operate, how efficiently it moves, and which tasks it can perform reliably.
Humanoids
Humanoids use human-like bodies—two legs, two arms, upright posture. Their advantage is environmental compatibility: they can operate in spaces designed for people without facility redesign. Warehouses, factories, and retail environments can accommodate humanoids with minimal retrofitting. They navigate stairs, doorways, and tight spaces that wheeled systems cannot.
The tradeoff is complexity and cost. Bipedal locomotion is energy-intensive and difficult to control. Two-armed manipulation increases failure modes. Battery life is constrained. While costs are declining with scale, humanoids remain expensive and operationally demanding. Most deployments today focus on narrow, repetitive tasks—tote handling, simple assembly—rather than general-purpose labor.
Industrial (Non Humanoid)
Industrial robots don’t resemble humans. They optimize for efficiency, reliability, and cost within structured environments.
Fixed robotic arms are the backbone of industrial automation—anchored systems that excel at repetitive, high-precision tasks like welding, palletizing, and assembly. Collaborative variants add sensing to operate safely near humans but still require structured workflows.
Mobile manipulators combine wheeled bases with robotic arms. Wheels handle navigation; arms perform manipulation. Mechanically efficient for flat, indoor environments, but limited in spaces requiring stairs or tight human-scale navigation.
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) focus purely on movement—wheeled platforms that transport materials within facilities. Their simplicity and clear productivity gains have driven widespread adoption.
Specialized form factors address niche environments: quadrupeds for uneven terrain, drones for inspection, soft robots for delicate handling. Each sacrifices generality for optimized performance in a narrow domain.
I learned with all form factors, there’s always some tradeoff between hyper-vertical, or hyper-specialized.
Layer 3: Vertical Use Cases
There are many different vertical applications across cleaning, construction, energy, agriculture, security, retail, healthcare, warehouse logistics, and industrial automation. I’ll talk about a few of the vertical use cases below.
Humanoid & General-Purpose Labor
Humanoids target environments designed for humans—warehouses, factories, retail—where facility redesign is impractical. The form factor promises versatility, but current deployments remain narrow: simple, repeatable manipulation tasks.
The landscape is differentiated by approach. Agility Robotics has the most mature commercial traction, with Digit moving over 100,000 totes at GXO warehouses. Figure AI is pursuing general-purpose manufacturing and logistics, anchored by its BMW partnership. Apptronik’s Apollo emphasizes modular, safety-focused industrial design. Sanctuary AI is betting on dexterity and cognitive task execution. 1X Technologies is building NEO for home assistance and light domestic chores—a different market entirely. Reflex Robotics takes a hybrid approach: a wheeled base (mechanically simpler than legs) with human-scale reach, optimized for warehouse workflows. Collaborative Robotics similarly uses a wheeled form factor designed to operate safely alongside humans in real facilities.
The open question is whether humanoids will justify their complexity. For many tasks, purpose-built form factors may win on cost and reliability. But for environments that can’t be restructured—and tasks that require human-scale manipulation—humanoids may be the only viable path.
Warehouse, Manufacturing, Logistics & Material Handling
E-commerce variability and persistent labor shortages have made logistics the proving ground for robotics. Seventy-six percent of logistics operations report labor constraints, and the ROI is clear: throughput gains, labor substitution, and 24/7 operation.
When I asked Jeff Mahler, CEO of Ambi Robotics, why he chose this category, he framed the scale of the opportunity: “There are over 1 trillion times a year that packages are touched by human hands on the way from the warehouse to someone’s front door.”
The landscape spans multiple sub-categories, each addressing different nodes in the logistics chain.
Picking and sorting is where most human touches occur. Ambi Robotics builds AI-powered robotic sorting systems for parcel and e-commerce fulfillment. Dexterity deploys mobile manipulation systems for truck unloading and complex picking, combining vision with tactile sensing. Dexterity’s flagship application is Truck loading, “which is extremely challenging because it involves being able to handle an infinite variation of randomly presented boxes, and requires a robot to learn how to play 4D box tetris across space and time”.
End-of-line automation handles the final steps of production—palletizing, packing, labeling, and preparing goods for shipment. Formic leads here with over 200,000 production hours at 99.8% uptime, charging $8–30 per hour with guaranteed ROI from day one. Seventy-five percent of their customers are automating for the first time.
Flexible robot arms bring automation to tasks that traditionally required custom engineering. Standard Bots builds AI-native six-axis arms in the U.S. that learn from demonstration—you move the arm through a task, and the system learns. Their RO1 costs half what comparable cobots do and deploys in hours, not months.
Software-defined manufacturing treats the factory floor like a programmable system. Bright Machines builds modular “microfactories”—robotic cells powered by computer vision, machine learning, and cloud-based orchestration. They’ve raised over $400 million and partnered with NVIDIA and Microsoft to focus on AI hardware infrastructure assembly.
Goods-to-person systems move inventory to workers rather than workers to inventory. Locus Robotics has scaled this model aggressively—over 5 billion picks across 350+ customer sites. Mytra takes a different approach: automated warehouse cells with bots and software optimized for heavy payload movement.
Material handling and transport automates the movement of pallets, carts, and containers within facilities. Vecna Robotics pairs AMRs with orchestration software for end-to-end workflows. Seegrid builds autonomous lift trucks for pallet movement. Third Wave Automation retrofits existing forklifts and tuggers with autonomy.
Yard and middle-mile operations extend automation beyond the warehouse walls. Outrider automates yard operations—moving trailers between dock doors and parking areas. Gatik runs autonomous box trucks on fixed B2B routes between distribution centers and retailers.
Retail inventory management sits at the edge of logistics. Simbe Robotics deploys Tally robots that scan retail aisles for inventory accuracy and pricing compliance—turning store floors into real-time data sources.
AI-powered manipulation enables robots to handle high-variability tasks without manual programming for each SKU. Covariant built the “Covariant Brain,” a foundation model trained on billions of robotic episodes that lets standard industrial arms recognize and handle millions of items. In 2024, Amazon hired its founders and licensed the technology—a signal of how valuable generalizable manipulation intelligence has become.
Construction Robotics
Construction faces acute skilled labor shortages—the industry needs nearly 800,000 workers over the next two years, and 40% of the workforce is nearing retirement. Robots must operate in dirty, unstructured, outdoor environments, but labor scarcity creates strong pull.
Autonomous heavy equipment tackles earthmoving and excavation. Bedrock Robotics raised $350 million, led by former Waymo engineers, and retrofits existing excavators and bulldozers with same-day installs. Built Robotics pioneered the space with its Exosystem kit, now deployed on solar projects with Bechtel and Mortenson.
3D-printed construction automates building structures. ICON has printed over 150 homes, raised $450 million, and holds a NASA contract for lunar construction.
Site layout translates digital plans to the physical jobsite. Dusty Robotics prints full-scale BIM drawings onto floors, reducing layout time by 68%.
Agriculture & Outdoor Robotics
Agriculture faces severe seasonal labor shortages, and repetitive outdoor tasks create viable automation economics despite environmental complexity. More than 70% of specialty crop growers have adopted some form of automation, driven by rising wages and a workforce down 40% in California over the past decade.
Harvest assistance augments human workers rather than replacing them. Burro, named Greenhouse Grower’s 2025 Technology of the Year, has 300+ robots following workers through specialty crops—grapes, berries, nurseries—autonomously hauling harvested produce back to pack lines. Raised $24 million Series B in early 2025 after logging 75,000 autonomous miles.
Farm data and vision turns tractors into AI-powered data collectors. Orchard Robotics raised $25 million for cameras that mount on existing vehicles and analyze fruit size, color, and health across billions of individual pieces.
Precision weeding eliminates herbicides through targeted weed removal. Carbon Robotics’ LaserWeeder uses AI to identify and kill weeds with lasers—over 10 billion eliminated since 2022, cutting weed control costs by 80%. Verdant Robotics takes a different approach with its SharpShooter, using “aim and apply” technology to deliver micro-liter doses with millimeter accuracy at 480 shots per second, reducing chemical inputs by 96%.
Autonomous platforms provide AI-first autonomy across equipment types. Bonsai Robotics raised $15 million in early 2025 and acquired farm-ng in July, combining vision-based autonomy software with modular electric robots. For commercial landscaping, Scythe Robotics builds 100+ electric autonomous mowers annually, now deploying across multiple states.
Controlled environment farming uses robots inside greenhouses. Iron Ox operates AI-powered facilities in California and Texas, with robots that lift 1,000-pound modules, scan crops, and deliver precise nutrients. Backed by Bill Gates’ Breakthrough Energy Ventures with $98 million raised.
Home, Food & Last-Mile Service Robots
General-purpose home assistance represents the holy grail. Sunday Robotics emerged from stealth in November 2025, and built a wheeled robot with dual arms trained on 10 million household episodes collected from 500+ homes via its Skill Capture Glove. The robot clears tables, loads dishwashers, folds laundry, and brews espresso—targeting sub-$10,000 pricing at scale, with 50 households selected for late-2026 beta. Matic raised $107 million for a premium floor-cleaning robot using computer vision instead of lidar.
Healthcare logistics has proven more tractable than homes. Diligent Robotics’ Moxi operates in 25+ hospitals, completing 1.25 million deliveries and 125,000 autonomous elevator rides. Labrador Systems deploys Retriever Pro AMRs in senior living—essentially mobile shelving that brings items within reach for residents with mobility limitations.
Restaurant automation targets the highest-turnover roles where annual employee churn exceeds 144%. Miso Robotics’ redesigned Flippy (late 2024) is half the size, processes 100 baskets/hour, and rents for $5,400/month—operators report $75,000 in annual savings per location. Travis Kalanick is also building a new company called Picnic.
Defense, Security & Autonomous Systems
Inspection of critical defense and industrial infrastructure is shifting from manual processes to persistent robotic monitoring. Gecko Robotics deploys climbing robots and AI software to inspect ships, aircraft carriers, power plants, and refineries, transforming physical assets into continuously digitized systems.
Physical security is increasingly automated as facilities scale and staffing becomes constrained. Cobalt Robotics provides autonomous security robots combined with remote human oversight to deliver 24/7 patrol and monitoring for defense installations, data centers, and sensitive industrial sites.
Autonomous operations in GPS- and communications-denied environments are becoming table stakes. Anduril is building a new defense prime around software-defined autonomy, delivering integrated systems across air, land, and sea that are unified by its Lattice command-and-control platform and already deployed with U.S. and allied forces. Shield AI develops the Hivemind autonomy stack, enabling aircraft and drones to navigate, coordinate, and execute missions independently when human control and external signals are unavailable.
Small autonomous aerial systems have become essential for reconnaissance, inspection, and tactical awareness. Skydio builds vision-based drones that fly without GPS or pilots using onboard perception, making them the dominant U.S. supplier for defense, public safety, and government inspection use cases.
Maritime autonomy is emerging as a core pillar of future naval strategy. Saronic is developing autonomous surface vessels designed for fleet-scale deployment, prioritizing low-cost, rapidly manufactured platforms that enable distributed and attritable naval operations.
Together, these companies show why defense is one of the clearest early markets for robotics & physical AI: a defined buyer, high willingness to pay, and missions where autonomy delivers immediate operational and strategic value rather than incremental efficiency.
Three Robotics Investment Theses for 2026
Today, Deployment Infrastructure Beats Model Intelligence
There’s a widespread assumption, particularly among investors coming from software, that once foundation models get good enough, robotics will experience its “ChatGPT moment” and adoption will explode.
The investor and founders I spoke to actually deploying robots disagree. Ambi’s Jim Liefer shares: “I disagree with the viewpoint that robotics will be solved in one giant leap, at some ‘ChatGPT moment,’ once models get sufficiently capable. The hard part about deploying robots to the real world isn’t making a robot that can do everything—it’s making robots that can rapidly adapt to do one thing very well, at a low cost.”
Ben from Goldman shared: “There are a number of companies that have emerged over the years that sit somewhere on the spectrum from ‘general-purpose’ to ‘developing a specific task.’ Companies move along that spectrum throughout their existence. Many started as software-only ‘brains’— very similar to what some are pitching now: general-purpose robotic intelligence. Eventually, they all realized you have to start with a specific task, and you probably need to be building on hardware. All of them would still say they’re not working on a single individual task, but they’ve started to build on hardware and actually develop a full solution. They all realized they need a solution, not just a model.”
One thesis I am exploring is that the opportunity in 2026 is betting on operators who can actually get robots into production and keep them running, not just model builders optimizing for benchmarks that don’t translate to factory floors?
Production Data Is the Best Compounding Moat
Every founder I spoke with converged on the same point: real-world deployment data is the defensible advantage, and there’s no shortcut to getting it.
In my interview with Ben Fife, Partner at Goldman Sachs Growth Equity Fund, where he covers robotics, he shared: “What every company eventually realizes in this space is that performing in a demo environment is very different from performing in production. The ability to operationalize the technology—to deliver something that both generates ROI for customers and is economically attractive for robotics companies—is extremely challenging. In many ways, it’s the hardest part of the entire problem”
One question today is, training data can be collected synthetically—through simulation, teleoperation, or watching videos of humans - does it work?
Formic’s Farid is direct: “In reality, real data collection at scale will only come from large-scale deployments. Whoever has the most robots in the field, soonest, will have the best data and the best AI models.”
Ambi’s Liefer explains why synthetic data falls short: “Just like humans, robots need practice doing a particular task in their own bodies before they work with high levels of reliability. If you’re learning to play golf, you can’t just watch videos and then go hit the course and expect to be Tiger Woods. You need to actually practice yourself, in your own body.” This creates a flywheel that’s difficult to replicate. Ambi again: “Production data creates a flywheel where AI improves, opening new opportunities to automate adjacent tasks, and builds the company’s reputation for high performance in production, helping to close other customers.”
Locus Robotics is already capturing this advantage: “As our existing fleet of robots is collecting more data every minute, we don’t need to rely so heavily on simulation—similar to Tesla having the benefit in FSD of having millions of cars on the road collecting datapoints.”
Bright Machines’ Sviat Dulianinov quantifies the problem for anyone trying to go general-purpose without deployment scale: “Collecting 10,000 data points for one specific task is fundamentally different from collecting 10,000 data points across 10 million different tasks. The former is tractable; the latter may not be economically viable for years.” The implication for 2026 is stark—companies without production deployments today are structurally disadvantaged regardless of their model capabilities.
The diligence question isn’t “how good is your model?” but “how many production hours do you have, at what uptime, with paying customers?”
Today, Purpose-Built Form Factors Beat Humanoids
The operators I spoke to are skeptical of general-purpose humanoids.
The core argument for humanoids is environmental compatibility. The entire built world—factories, warehouses, homes, retail stores—was designed for human bodies. Stairs, doorways, workstations, tools, shelves: all optimized for bipedal creatures with two arms and roughly six feet of reach. Purpose-built robots require facility redesign or can only operate in narrow zones. Humanoids, in theory, drop into existing infrastructure without retrofitting. That’s not a small thing when you’re talking about millions of brownfield facilities.
There’s also the generalization argument. Specialized robots do one thing well, but scaling means deploying different systems for different tasks—AMRs for transport, arms for picking, separate systems for packing. A sufficiently capable humanoid could handle all three, reducing fleet complexity and integration overhead. If foundation models deliver on cross-task transfer learning, the humanoid form factor is the natural beneficiary: one body that can be reprogrammed for new work rather than new hardware for each use case.
Jonathan Hurst from Agility Robotics makes the strongest case I’ve heard: warehouses and factories are laid out for people, so you want a narrow, dynamically balanced base that can move through hallways and doors, lift 25kg loads, reach from the floor to high shelves, and communicate intent to nearby workers. As he puts it: “The only reason you would add a head is because you have a human centric machine. It’s an opportunity to communicate with people on their terms. Because you can have very simple expressions with just a pair of eyes like we’ve got that just blink show a direction of where the robot’s about to go, show its intent, and convey things in a way that requires no training.”
But even Hurst acknowledges the form factor doesn’t need to perfectly mimic biology: “I think that in the future, when we look back on this era of innovation, it’s gonna be kind of analogous to now we look back at the beginning of flight where we saw people strapping these flapping wings and even gluing feathers to things to try and figure out how to make something that can fly. Fundamentally, there’s a lot of similarities. Right? Airplanes have wings, but you don’t need feathers. I don’t think that the five fingered hands that everybody’s building are gonna be a thing for very long.”
That caveat matters because it opens the door to a different question: if you’re already engineering away from human morphology where it’s inefficient, why constrain yourself to the bipedal form at all?
Formic’s Farid frames it as a question of ambition: “Robots should provide superhuman performance, not human-equivalent performance. It follows then that some robots should have six arms, and some robots should have wheels instead of legs, and some robots should be taller than a building in order to truly transform what humanity is capable of. I think humanoids are appealing but ultimately a red herring.”
Locus Robotics’ perspective comes from operational reality: “It doesn’t make sense for a bipedal humanoid to spend large amounts of time doing transport across a warehouse that could be done more efficiently via a conveyor belt or autonomous mobile robot. So long as the hardware is efficiently busy doing the work that humans would otherwise do—ideally 18+ hours per day—this is optimal versus more general hardware which may be able to perform these same tasks much less efficiently.”
Miso’s Richard Hull didn’t mince words on timeline: “Humanoid robots are easily a decade away from safe, reliable, autonomous operation in the mainstream.”
Bright Machines’ Dulianinov points to the capital required, using Waymo as a benchmark: “They’ve spent an estimated $8-10 billion just to get autonomous vehicles working in the relatively constrained environment of city streets, where there are traffic rules, stop signs, and predictable patterns. General-purpose humanoid robots operating in completely unstructured environments face an exponentially harder problem.”
Ambi’s Liefer offers the one nuance—specialized systems win in industrial settings “where saving pennies and milliseconds matter,” while general systems may eventually find a home in consumer environments with “constantly changing needs.”
The humanoid thesis requires believing that generalization value exceeds specialization efficiency, and that the cost and reliability gaps close faster than the skeptics expect. For 2026, the opportunity is clear: task-optimized systems already generating ROI for customers, not versatile platforms waiting for their use case to emerge. If humanoids start posting production hours and uptime metrics that rival the specialized players, the calculus changes.
Where to Deploy Capital in 2026?
The investment opportunity in robotics today isn’t about betting on the most ambitious technical vision, it’s about backing operators who are already solving the deployment problem at scale.
Look for companies running production fleets with measurable uptime, not lab demos. Prioritize businesses where the RaaS model has proven unit economics and customers are renewing or expanding deployments. Focus on verticals where labor economics have fundamentally broken—warehouses running 24/7 to keep pace with e-commerce volatility, manufacturers losing workers faster than they can hire.
The foundation model companies and humanoid platforms may eventually prove transformative. But in 2026, the safer growth stage bet is on the operators who’ve already crossed the chasm from research to reliable revenue, and are using that traction to build moats that pure-play model builders can’t easily replicate.
Robotics doesn’t need a ChatGPT moment. It needs more robots in production, generating compounding advantages for the companies that figure out deployment first.

Jonathan, this is the most operationally honest robotics piece I've read this cycle. The "snowball, not ChatGPT moment" framing maps exactly to what we see on the IoT infrastructure side.
The RaaS model shift is the real unlock, and here's the connectivity dimension that connects your three investment theses: when you sell outcomes instead of hardware, you're implicitly selling an uptime SLA. And uptime at scale requires a connectivity and fleet management stack that most robotics companies are dramatically underinvesting in.
Consider Formic's 99.8% uptime across 200,000+ production hours. That number isn't just about mechanical reliability -- it requires real-time health monitoring, predictive maintenance signals flowing from edge sensors to cloud analytics, and rapid remote diagnostics when something degrades. At $8-30/hour per robot, even 0.2% downtime has measurable revenue impact. The connectivity infrastructure to maintain that SLA across hundreds of customer sites with different network environments is a significant operational moat in itself.
Your production data thesis resonates deeply. But there's a data transport problem embedded in it: getting high-fidelity sensor data from deployed fleets back to training pipelines isn't trivial. A robot generating camera, lidar, tactile, and joint-state data at production rates can produce gigabytes per shift. Batching, compressing, and reliably transmitting that over facility networks with competing traffic is its own engineering challenge -- especially in food processing or agriculture where connectivity infrastructure is minimal.
The purpose-built vs. humanoid debate also has a connectivity angle. Specialized robots in structured environments can often use facility Ethernet or WiFi. Humanoids operating in unstructured environments (homes, construction sites) will need resilient cellular connectivity with carrier failover -- eSIM orchestration becomes critical when your robot needs to operate across different network environments without human intervention.
Hugo's valuation-to-deployment-hours metric in the comments is sharp. I'd add a companion: cost-per-connected-robot-hour. That number will separate the companies that can scale from those that can't.
